question.worked_solution:
Since the logarithms on both sides of the equation have the same base, we can equate the arguments. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{x}^{2}-2) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x) \\ 2{x}^{2}-2 & =3x \\ 2{x}^{2}-3x-2 & =0 \\ (2x+1)(x-2) & =0 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{2},2.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now check for extraneous solutions by substituting back into the original equation: 

- Substituting $x=\frac{1}{2}$ back into the original equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{x}^{2}-2) & \overset{?}{=}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-2) & \overset{?}{=}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3\cdot (\frac{1}{2})) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(-\frac{3}{2}) & \overset{?}{=}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{2})\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

which is not valid because $\operatorname{ln}⁡(-\frac{3}{2})$ is undefined. Therefore, $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ is not a valid solution.

- Substituting $x=2$ back into the original equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{x}^{2}-2) & \overset{?}{=}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot {(2)}^{2}-2) & \overset{?}{=}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3\cdot (2)) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(6) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(6).\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=2$ is a valid solution.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$x=2$ only."
